traveler: Diego María de la Concepción Juan Nepomuceno Estanislao de la Rivera y Barrientos Acosta y Rodríguez (Diego Rivera)
title: The Chalkboard Walls: Guanajuato, Montparnasse, and the Painting of a Nation
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Silver City and the Academy

stops.name: Guanajuato, birth on the Calle de Positos
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In a tall stone house on the Calle de Positos, in a silver city cut into a ravine, a son is born to Diego Rivera Acosta and Maria del Pilar Barrientos. He arrives a twin; his brother Carlos dies before turning two. The boy draws before he can spell, and rather than keep scrubbing the walls his parents line them with chalkboards. Guanajuato is the cradle he names for the rest of his life, though his father's mining ventures fail and the family leaves while he is still small. The house becomes a museum in September 1975, long after every Rivera has gone from it.
suggested_refs: Museo Casa Diego Rivera, Positos 47, Guanajuato
sources: Patrick Marnham, Dreaming with His Eyes Open

stops.name: Mexico City, the family arrives near the Alameda
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: The mining ventures collapse and the Riveras come down to the capital, settling within walking distance of the Alameda Central, the colonial promenade where the city takes its Sunday air. The family loses its provincial standing in the move. The boy gets the schools and museums of a capital. He will leave this city for Madrid, for Paris, for Moscow, for Detroit, and come back from each of them. Fifty-three years later he paints this park onto a wall and puts himself into it as a child, holding the hand of a skeleton.
suggested_refs: The Alameda Central, Mexico City, subject of the 1946-47 Hotel del Prado mural
sources: Marnham, Dreaming with His Eyes Open
Bertram D. Wolfe, The Fabulous Life of Diego Rivera

stops.name: Academia de San Carlos, the student years
stops.date_confidence: contested: the chronology has him entering at about age ten, i.e. 1896-97; a parallel account gives the range 1898-1905. Not reconciled here
stops.campa: At about ten he enters the Academia de San Carlos, oldest art academy in the Americas, and copies plaster casts and old canvases under masters trained in Europe, Jose Maria Velasco among them. The classicism chafes by his teens; the drawing never leaves him. He is a student in this city in 1904, the year he will later claim he and others pooled their money to buy cadavers from the morgue and ate them. His biographers treat the story as an elaborate lie he preferred to a plainer youth. In 1907 he leaves for Europe on state money.
stops.quote: I believe that when man evolves a civilization higher than the mechanized but still primitive one he has now, the eating of human flesh will be sanctioned. For then man will have thrown off all of his superstitions and irrational taboos.
stops.quote_source: Diego Rivera with Gladys March, My Art, My Life: An Autobiography (Citadel Press, 1960; Dover reprint 1991), p. 20. Wikipedia's own summary notes the underlying anecdote 'has been considered factually suspect or an elaborate lie'
suggested_refs: The Academia de San Carlos, Calle Academia 22, Mexico City
sources: Marnham, Dreaming with His Eyes Open

stops.name: Veracruz, the ship for Spain
stops.date_confidence: month attested (January 1907); day unknown, defaulted to the first
stops.campa: He boards ship at Veracruz at twenty, carrying a pension from Teodoro Dehesa, governor of the state, and an earlier stipend from Justo Sierra that the shorter accounts leave out. He has never left Mexico. The crossing runs weeks; behind him is an academy of plaster casts, ahead a Madrid he knows only by the name of the painter he means to study under. He will be gone thirteen years. What he brings back from them is fresco, a medium no painter in Mexico is then working at scale.
suggested_refs: The port of Veracruz, point of departure for the 1907 European pension

segments.name: The Prado, La Ruche, and the Cubist Decade

stops.name: Museo del Prado, Madrid: the second academy
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Madrid year 1907; the Toledo excursion inside it is traditional and undated in the major biographies
stops.campa: He studies formally under Eduardo Chicharro and spends his real hours inside the Prado, copying Goya and Velazquez off the wall. The dark galleries are his second academy, and he will credit Goya's black paintings with teaching him more than any classroom did. He goes down to Toledo to see El Greco in the city that made him, and finds a painter working inside his own landscape, a lesson he applies literally twenty years later on the walls of Mexican buildings. Before Madrid he had seen the old masters only in reproduction.
suggested_refs: The Goya rooms of the Museo del Prado
The Church of Santo Tome, Toledo
sources: Marnham, Dreaming with His Eyes Open

stops.name: Bruges, the meeting with Angelina Beloff
stops.date_confidence: contested: some accounts place the meeting in Bruges, Marnham in Brussels; the year 1909 follows the Beloff record. Month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: On a journey north from Paris he meets the Russian painter Angelina Beloff. One account puts the meeting in Bruges and another in Brussels, and the standard literature does not reconcile them. She becomes his companion through the poorest Paris years and bears him a son. Some sources call her his wife, others his common-law wife; the union is dated to the end of 1909 in one place and to 1911 in another, and several biographers hold there was never a legal marriage at all.
suggested_refs: The contradictory Bruges and Brussels accounts of the Rivera-Beloff meeting
sources: Marnham, Dreaming with His Eyes Open

stops.name: La Ruche, Passage de Dantzig, Paris
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: He arrives in Paris and goes to La Ruche, the circular iron hive at 2 Passage de Dantzig salvaged from the 1900 Exposition Universelle and cut into cheap studios. Chagall, Soutine, Modigliani, Leger, Zadkine and Archipenko pass through the same staircases in these years. The building stands in the fifteenth arrondissement, in Vaugirard, and not in the Montparnasse the shorter accounts assign it; Montparnasse is a walk away and it is where the arguments happen. He takes a room and begins the decade that makes him a Cubist.
suggested_refs: La Ruche, 2 Passage de Dantzig, Paris XV
sources: Marnham, Dreaming with His Eyes Open

stops.name: Paris, the union with Beloff and the record that fights itself
stops.date_confidence: contested: 1911 per the Rivera infobox (with divorce 1921); the Beloff article says they married in Paris by the end of 1909; several biographers hold the union was never legal. Month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: The atlas pins Paris at a single coordinate and Rivera lives inside it for twelve years. In 1911 he and Angelina Beloff are recorded as married, though the record fights itself: one account has them married here by the end of 1909, the infobox gives 1911 and a divorce in 1921, and several biographers say the union was never legal at all. He paints, and through most of those years he has no money. Twenty-eight years later Frida Kahlo sails to this same pin for the Mexique exhibition Marcel Duchamp assembles, and Picasso, Kandinsky and Duchamp stand in front of her work.
suggested_refs: The canonical atlas Paris pin, shared with the Kahlo file

stops.name: Rue du Depart 26, Montparnasse: the Cubist studio
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period 1913-1917; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: He keeps a studio on the Rue du Depart above the Gare Montparnasse, in the few blocks where Picasso's circle also works. The canvases go tight and faceted, indebted to Picasso and Gris; in 1914 Amedeo Modigliani, who drinks in the same cafes, paints his portrait. He argues painting at the Dome and the Rotonde with Russians and Spaniards waiting out a war. Around 1917 he breaks with Cubism in public, after a quarrel with the critic Pierre Reverdy, and begins moving toward the legible, monumental manner that walls will require of him.
suggested_refs: Modigliani's 1914 portraits of Rivera
The Cafe du Dome, Boulevard du Montparnasse
sources: PBS American Experience, Diego Rivera timeline

stops.name: Rue du Depart, the son named Diego
stops.date_confidence: birth 1916 attested, death 1918 attested; sources that give a single date conflate the two. Month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Angelina Beloff bears him a son in 1916 and they name him Diego. The child dies at fourteen months of lung complications, in 1918, in a Paris with no coal; the shorter accounts compress the dates and say he died in infancy the year he was born. In 1919 the painter Marevna, Maria Vorobieff-Stebelska, bears him a daughter, Marika. He acknowledges neither household fully. By 1918 the break from Cubism is complete and the work turns figurative and Renaissance-facing. What he wants now is Italy.
suggested_refs: Marevna's memoirs of Montparnasse and the birth of Marika Rivera in 1919
sources: PBS American Experience, Diego Rivera timeline

segments.name: Italy, and the Walls of the Republic

stops.name: Santa Maria Novella, Florence: learning the wall
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1920 Italian study year; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: He crosses into Italy and spends the year standing in front of walls. In Florence he studies the fresco cycles: Ghirlandaio's Tornabuoni Chapel at Santa Maria Novella, Masaccio's Trinity in the same church and his Brancacci frescoes across the river at the Carmine. He fills notebooks with composition and gesture and almost no color, learning how a painted wall organizes a crowd of bodies across architecture. Nobody teaches him this. He works it out standing in front of the walls, and in 1922 he starts using it.
suggested_refs: Ghirlandaio's Tornabuoni Chapel; Masaccio's Trinity, Santa Maria Novella
sources: PBS American Experience, Diego Rivera timeline
Marnham, Dreaming with His Eyes Open

stops.name: Basilica di San Francesco, Assisi: Giotto
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Italian itinerary is rebuilt from later interviews and sketchbooks, not from a dated day-by-day record. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He goes down to Assisi for Giotto in the Basilica di San Francesco, the cycle that Europe by then calls the founding moment of narrative painting on plaster. The Italian itinerary is reconstructed from later interviews and surviving sketchbooks rather than from a day-by-day record, so the individual stops are well supported and not documentarily fixed. What is fixed is the outcome. He returns to Mexico in 1921 already committed to fresco, a medium no living Mexican painter is then practicing at scale.
suggested_refs: The Giotto cycle, Upper Church, Basilica of San Francesco d'Assisi
sources: Marnham, Dreaming with His Eyes Open

stops.name: Basilica di San Vitale, Ravenna: the gold ground
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, same Italian tour; rests on Rivera's own later testimony rather than dated correspondence. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: In Ravenna he stands under the Byzantine mosaics of San Vitale and in the small dark vault of Galla Placidia: gold ground, flat hieratic figures, faces turned frontally out at whoever enters. Assisi gives him the storytelling and Ravenna gives him the stare. The peasants and workers on the Mexican walls will face out of the plaster the same way, at whoever walks in. Like the rest of the Italian tour the stop rests on his own later testimony, and the literature treats it as strongly likely rather than proved.
suggested_refs: The mosaics of San Vitale and the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia, Ravenna

stops.name: San Ildefonso, Mexico City: the first mural
stops.date_confidence: attested (January 1922); the mural is unveiled in 1923
stops.campa: Under the education minister Jose Vasconcelos he paints his first mural, Creation, in the Bolivar Amphitheatre of the old Jesuit college of San Ildefonso. He works in encaustic, not true fresco, still learning the medium, and abandons the technique afterward. It is unveiled in 1923 to a divided city. A schoolgirl named Frida Kahlo watches him from the courtyard. Fourteen years later Antonin Artaud lectures in this same building, under the murals of Orozco, hunting a Mexico he has crossed an ocean to find.
suggested_refs: The Bolivar Amphitheatre, Antiguo Colegio de San Ildefonso

stops.name: Secretaria de Educacion Publica: six years of courtyards
stops.date_confidence: attested: begun September 1922, finished 1928
stops.campa: In September he begins the two courtyards of the Secretariat of Public Education and does not finish for six years: one hundred and twenty-four fresco panels of labor, festival, harvest and revolution, region by region across Mexico. He works with a team, learns true fresco here, and joins the Mexican Communist Party partway through. It is the largest surviving concentration of his work. In the same year he divorces Angelina Beloff in June and marries Guadalupe Marin, and helps found the union of technical workers, painters and sculptors.
suggested_refs: The two courtyards of the SEP building, Calle Republica de Argentina 28

stops.name: Chapingo, the chapel of the fertile earth
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1924-1927; a looser 1925-1927 range circulates. Month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: At the National School of Agriculture he takes a deconsecrated hacienda chapel and fills it, walls and ceiling, with forty-one panels over seven hundred square meters: nude allegories of germination and the fertile earth in a room built for a different god. The principal panel is Tierra Fecunda. He runs it alongside the Secretariat commission and uses it to work a single unified space rather than a corridor of separate scenes. The university keeps the chapel as a protected monument and the nudes stay on its walls.
suggested_refs: The former hacienda chapel, Universidad Autonoma Chapingo

segments.name: Moscow, and the Elephant and the Dove

stops.name: Red Square, Moscow: the tenth anniversary
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1927; day unknown, defaulted to the first
stops.campa: He travels to Moscow with a delegation invited for the tenth anniversary of the October Revolution and stands in Red Square among the crowds and the banners. He meets Soviet painters and officials and, separately, a young American curator named Alfred Barr, who will bring him to New York four years later. The trip hardens his formal Communist commitment and exposes him to the factional weather inside the Party, which within months makes him suspect in Moscow and, not long after, at home.
suggested_refs: The 1927 October Revolution decennial celebrations, Moscow
sources: PBS American Experience, Diego Rivera timeline
MoMA institutional history of the Barr-Rivera relationship

stops.name: Krasnaya Presnya, Moscow: the commission he is not allowed to finish
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the building is not identified in the sources reachable here and the pin is district-level only. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: He is commissioned to paint a mural for a Red Army club in Moscow and is ordered out of the Soviet Union before it amounts to much, under suspicion of political unreliability. How much paint reached the wall is disputed, and the building itself is not identified in the sources reachable here, so the pin sits in a district and not on a door. He returns to Mexico in 1928 with an unfinished commission behind him and is expelled from the Mexican Communist Party the following year, by the Party he crossed an ocean to celebrate.
suggested_refs: The unlocated Red Army club commission, Moscow 1927-28
sources: Marnham, Dreaming with His Eyes Open (building unidentified)

stops.name: The SEP scaffold: Frida Kahlo climbs up with three canvases
stops.date_confidence: contested: sources place the first meeting variously in 1922, when she watched him at San Ildefonso, and in 1928 at the SEP scaffold. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: A young woman with a broken spine climbs the scaffold at the Secretariat carrying three canvases and asks him, without preamble, whether she has talent or should find other work. He comes down and looks. Sources put the first meeting anywhere between 1922 and 1928 and do not agree with each other. He is forty-one and married; she is twenty-one and paints lying down. Her own journey is already in the atlas, and it enters his life at this scaffold.
stops.quote: an unusual energy of expression, precise delineation of character, and true severity ... They had a fundamental plastic honesty, and an artistic personality of their own ... It was obvious to me that this girl was an authentic artist.
stops.quote_source: Rivera's recollection of first seeing Frida Kahlo's paintings, c. 1928, quoted in Hayden Herrera, Frida: A Biography of Frida Kahlo (2002 ed.), pp. 86-87
suggested_refs: The SEP courtyard scaffold, site of the Rivera-Kahlo meeting

stops.name: Casa Azul, Coyoacan: the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: They marry in Coyoacan, in a cobalt house on the Calle Londres that is her father's and her birthplace. He is forty-two and she is twenty-two, and her mother calls it the marriage of an elephant and a dove. The ground under the house is old: Hernan Cortes made Coyoacan his headquarters in 1521 and had Cuauhtemoc tortured here for gold, four centuries before anyone painted a wall blue. Rivera will marry her twice, divorce her once, outlive her by three years, and end as the custodian of this address.
suggested_refs: The Casa Azul, Calle Londres, Coyoacan, later the Museo Frida Kahlo

stops.name: Palacio de Cortes, Cuernavaca: the conquest on the conqueror's wall
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1929-1930; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: The departing American ambassador Dwight Morrow pays for a mural history of Morelos across the loggia of the Palacio de Cortes, the oldest colonial civil building in the Americas, raised by Cortes himself on the platform of a Tlahuica temple. Rivera paints the conquest onto the conqueror's own house and ends the cycle with Emiliano Zapata leading a white horse, an image reproduced past counting. The commission and the marriage begin in the same season, and an American diplomat is paying for both the paint and the goodwill.
suggested_refs: The loggia murals of the Palacio de Cortes, Cuernavaca

stops.name: Pacific Stock Exchange, San Francisco: the first American commission
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1930; day unknown, defaulted to the first
stops.campa: His first commission in the United States, arranged by the architect Timothy Pflueger, is an allegory of California's soil and industry for the Luncheon Club inside the Pacific Stock Exchange, painted for a fee of two thousand five hundred dollars while local artists protest that a Mexican Communist has been handed an American wall. He arrives with Kahlo, his third wife; she meets the surgeon Leo Eloesser in this city and will come back to him for treatment. The mural is still on its original stairwell landing, never moved and never damaged.
suggested_refs: Allegory of California, City Club stairwell, 155 Sansome Street
sources: City Club of San Francisco records

stops.name: California School of Fine Arts: a fresco about making a fresco
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: At the California School of Fine Arts on Chestnut Street he paints The Making of a Fresco Showing the Building of a City, and puts the scaffolding, the assistants and his own broad back inside the picture. The subject of the fresco is the making of the fresco, hands and scaffolding left in. He and Kahlo live partly out of the sculptor Ralph Stackpole's studio. The work stays in the building, and the Bay Area muralists of the Depression years work in its shadow for a decade afterward.
suggested_refs: The Making of a Fresco, San Francisco Art Institute, 800 Chestnut Street
sources: San Francisco Art Institute institutional records

stops.name: The Heckscher Building, New York: the MoMA retrospective
stops.date_confidence: contested: the research pool gives 1931-11, which is when Rivera arrived in New York; MoMA's own exhibition record gives 23 December 1931 to 27 January 1932. moma.org returned HTTP 403 to the research session and was not re-verified
stops.campa: The Museum of Modern Art gives him a retrospective, only its second one-artist show after Matisse, arranged in part through Alfred Barr, whom he met in Moscow. The museum is not yet on Fifty-Third Street; it is renting floors of the Heckscher Building at 730 Fifth Avenue and will not reach its permanent house until 1939. He arrives in November and paints portable frescoes on movable steel frames for the show itself. The crowds are enormous. Detroit and Rockefeller Center are eighteen months away.
suggested_refs: MoMA exhibition 1745, 'Diego Rivera', 23 December 1931 - 27 January 1932
sources: MoMA exhibition records (moma.org/calendar/exhibitions/1745, HTTP 403 this session)

stops.name: Detroit Institute of Arts: twenty-seven panels of the Rouge
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1932-1933; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: For eleven months he and his assistants cover the four walls of the museum's inner court with twenty-seven fresco panels of the Ford Rouge plant: blast furnace, assembly line, stamping press, the vaccination panel, workers' bodies arranged the way a Last Judgment arranges the dead. Edsel Ford pays. Rivera sketches inside the Rouge before he paints a line. In a hospital a few miles away Frida Kahlo miscarries and begins the paintings that will make her name. The cycle survives whole and has never been moved.
stops.quote: Your engineers are your great artists, and these highways are the most beautiful things I have seen in your beautiful country. Out of them and the machine will issue the style of tomorrow.
stops.quote_source: Recalled by Bertram D. Wolfe as said to him personally: Wolfe, The Fabulous Life of Diego Rivera / Diego Rivera: His Life and Times. Wikiquote's citation to a Yale-New Haven curriculum unit is dead and should be dropped
suggested_refs: Rivera Court, Detroit Institute of Arts
sources: Detroit Institute of Arts institutional records

stops.name: Rockefeller Center, New York: the wall that is chiselled off
stops.date_confidence: attested: proposed January 1932, contracted November 1932, painting begun March 1933, work halted 10 May 1933, mural destroyed February 1934
stops.campa: Abby Aldrich Rockefeller proposes him for the RCA Building lobby in January 1932; the contract is signed that November and he begins painting in March 1933. He puts Lenin's face among the figures. Ordered to take it out, he offers to add Lincoln instead and refuses to remove Lenin; on the tenth of May Hugh Robertson stops the work, Rivera is paid his twenty-one thousand dollars in full and barred from the building. In February 1934 the wall is chiselled and the mural carried out in pieces. Photographs taken before the demolition are all that survive.
stops.quote: ... rather than mutilate the conception, I should prefer the physical destruction of the conception in its entirety, but preserving, at least, its integrity.
stops.quote_source: Letter of 6 May 1933 sent over Rivera's signature to Nelson Rockefeller (drafted, per Daniel Okrent, Great Fortune, by Ben Shahn). Wording per Rivera, My Art, My Life, and Bertram D. Wolfe; some editions read 'composition' for 'conception'
suggested_refs: Lucienne Bloch's clandestine photographs of Man at the Crossroads before its destruction

stops.name: Palacio de Bellas Artes: the mural repainted with the censor in it
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: He returns to Mexico in December 1933 and repaints the destroyed wall under a new title, Man, Controller of the Universe. Lenin goes back in. So does John D. Rockefeller Jr., drinking in a nightclub beneath a field of syphilis spirochetes. This is the version the public sees, since New York's was carried out in a wheelbarrow. The second version stands at full scale in the national fine arts palace, on a government wall, and it is still there. New York keeps photographs.
suggested_refs: Man, Controller of the Universe, Palacio de Bellas Artes, Mexico City
sources: INBA / Palacio de Bellas Artes records

segments.name: The National Palace and the Guest in Coyoacan

stops.name: Casa Estudio San Angel: two houses and a bridge
stops.date_confidence: built 1931-1932, occupied 1934; month and day of the move unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: Juan O'Gorman builds two functionalist houses at the corner of Altavista, one for Rivera and one for Kahlo, joined by a bridge across the roofs, so that each of them can work without the other in the room. Construction runs from 1931 to 1932 and the couple move in during 1934. He works in the larger cube for twenty-three years, keeps his papier mache Judases and his pre-Hispanic stone in it, and dies in it. It opens to the public as a museum on the sixteenth of December 1986.
suggested_refs: Museo Casa Estudio Diego Rivera y Frida Kahlo, Diego Rivera 2 esq. Altavista, San Angel
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Museo Casa Estudio Diego Rivera y Frida Kahlo'

stops.name: Palacio Nacional, the staircase: Mexico through the centuries
stops.date_confidence: attested for the staircase campaign 1929-1935; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: Across the main staircase of the seat of the Mexican presidency he paints the history of the country from before the conquest to the revolution, one continuous panorama that the government's own clerks walk past every morning. The staircase campaign runs from 1929 to 1935 and it is the most visited thing he ever makes. In the year he finishes it he tells an interviewer that his Jewishness is the dominant element in his life, a descent his biographers argue over and which appears nowhere on any wall he paints.
stops.quote: My Jewishness is the dominant element in my life.
stops.quote_source: Rivera, 1935, cited in Jennifer Lipman, 'On this day: Diego Rivera dies, November 24 1957', The Jewish Chronicle, 24 November 2010. The chain of custody runs through journalism, not the 1935 document
suggested_refs: Mexico Through the Centuries, main staircase, Palacio Nacional

stops.name: Casa Azul, Coyoacan: asylum for Trotsky
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: Rivera petitions President Lazaro Cardenas and wins asylum in Mexico for Leon Trotsky, expelled from the Soviet Union and refused by every other government on earth. Trotsky and Natalia Sedova move into the blue house in Coyoacan and live there under guard until 1939. Kahlo and Trotsky have an affair inside the arrangement. In 1940 an assassin reaches Trotsky with an ice axe four streets away. Fourteen years after that a young Argentine named Ernesto Guevara describes this city as the city of Trotsky's tomb.
suggested_refs: The fortified Blue House of the Trotsky years, Coyoacan, 1937-1939
sources: Standard biographical accounts of Rivera and Trotsky

stops.name: Coyoacan, the Manifesto for an Independent Revolutionary Art
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: Andre Breton comes to Mexico and the three of them draft a manifesto for an independent revolutionary art inside the blue house: no art in the service of a state, no commissar standing over a painter. It goes out signed by Breton and Rivera, and Trotsky, who wrote much of Rivera's half, keeps his own name off it. The document is one of the few places where Rivera's prose rather than his wall makes the argument. Within a year he has broken with Trotsky and Kahlo has divorced him.
suggested_refs: Manifesto for an Independent Revolutionary Art, Coyoacan, 1938
sources: Wikipedia, 'Manifesto for an Independent Revolutionary Art'

stops.name: Mexico City, the divorce
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: They divorce in 1939, thirteen months before they remarry. He keeps painting; she sails to Paris for the Mexique exhibition and comes back to a house she now holds alone. No two accounts of the divorce agree on its cause, and the two of them give different reasons at different times to different friends. Their files cross this coordinate a dozen times each. The remarriage will come with terms written into it: separate houses, and money kept separate.
suggested_refs: The 1939 divorce decree, Mexico City

segments.name: Pan American Unity and the Late Walls

stops.name: Treasure Island, San Francisco: painting in front of the crowd
stops.date_confidence: attested: begun 5 June 1940, complete by 29 November 1940. The coordinate is the Treasure Island exposition site and is not fixed to a fairground plan in the research pool
stops.campa: He paints the Golden Gate International Exposition mural in public, on a scaffold, with the fairgoers watching him work, for a thousand dollars a month: ten panels marrying the machinery of the north to the sculpture of the south, Coatlicue fused with a stamping press. He begins on the fifth of June and finishes by the twenty-ninth of November. The mural spends decades at City College of San Francisco, goes on show at SFMOMA in June 2021, and is taken apart in 2024 into storage at an undisclosed location on the college campus.
stops.quote: Here it is—the might, the power, the energy, the sadness, the glory, the youthfulness of our lands.
stops.quote_source: Rivera on the American scene, in Bertram D. Wolfe, The Fabulous Life of Diego Rivera, p. 278 (em dash as printed). Wikiquote's gloss attaching the line to New York City is unsupported by the corroborating texts, which are industry and automobile histories
suggested_refs: Pan American Unity, painted at Treasure Island 1940; at CCSF, then SFMOMA 2021-2024

stops.name: San Francisco, the second marriage to Frida Kahlo
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: They marry a second time in San Francisco on his fifty-fourth birthday, thirteen months after the divorce, with Leo Eloesser's medical advice somewhere behind it and separate houses written into the understanding. The pin is the atlas's San Francisco, the same financial district blocks where he painted his first American wall ten years before for a room in which stockbrokers ate their lunch. He will not be married to anyone else while she is alive.
suggested_refs: The 8 December 1940 remarriage, San Francisco

stops.name: Casa Azul, the pyramid in the garden
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: He raises a stepped pyramid of volcanic stone in the garden of the blue house and sets pre-Hispanic figures into its terraces, so that the courtyard where Kahlo grew up becomes an argument about what Mexico is. He is buying pre-Hispanic pieces at a rate that will end in more than forty thousand objects. Cortes camped on this ground in 1521. Trotsky read his mail here in 1938. Now there is a pyramid in it, built in the twentieth century by a painter, out of the same lava the whole valley is made of.
suggested_refs: The stepped pyramid in the garden of the Casa Azul, Coyoacan

stops.name: Anahuacalli, the black pyramid on the lava
stops.date_confidence: construction begins 1942 (Spanish and English records agree); month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: On the lava field south of Coyoacan he begins building a black basalt pyramid to hold his collection and, he intends, his ashes: not a museum so much as a temple raised for a dead civilization by a man with no commission and no patron for it. Construction runs from 1942 until his death and stops unfinished. His daughter Ruth Rivera completes it with Juan O'Gorman and Heriberto Pagelson; it opens to the public on the eighteenth of September 1964, seven years after the man who quarried it stops paying the masons.
suggested_refs: Museo Anahuacalli, Coyoacan, opened 18 September 1964

stops.name: Palacio Nacional, the corridors: the world before the conquest
stops.date_confidence: 1944-1952 per the Spanish-language record; a widely repeated 1942-1951 range is not supported there. Month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: He comes back to the National Palace for the corridor panels and paints the world before the conquest: the market of Tlatelolco seen from above, the maguey harvest, the dyers and the featherworkers, cities intact and working. The campaign runs from 1944 to 1952, eight years spent reconstructing a Mexico no living person has seen, largely out of the objects piling up in his own collection. The staircase covers the whole history. The corridors stay inside the part of it the conquest ended, in the building where the government sits.
suggested_refs: The pre-Hispanic corridor panels, Palacio Nacional, 1944-1952

stops.name: Hotel del Prado, the Alameda painted from memory
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1946-1947; month and day unknown, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: For the Versalles dining room of the Hotel del Prado he paints a fifteen-metre Sunday afternoon in the Alameda Central, the park he was brought to at six: four centuries of Mexican dead promenading together, with himself at about ten holding the hand of a Catrina skeleton, Jose Guadalupe Posada on her other arm and Kahlo standing behind him. He letters the words God does not exist onto Ignacio Ramirez's page. The mural is kept covered for years. The 1985 earthquake takes the hotel and the mural is moved into a building made for it.
stops.quote: To affirm 'God does not exist,' I do not have to hide behind Don Ignacio Ramirez; I am an atheist and I consider religions to be a form of collective neurosis.
stops.quote_source: Rivera on the Alameda mural controversy, quoted in Philip Stein, Siqueiros: His Life and Works (International Publishers, 1994), p. 176. The source gives no precise date, only 'nine years later' than the mural, i.e. roughly the mid-1950s
suggested_refs: Museo Mural Diego Rivera, built for the relocated Alameda mural
sources: Stein, Siqueiros: His Life and Works

stops.name: Casa Azul, the death of Frida Kahlo
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: She dies in the blue house at forty-seven, days after being wheeled into a street demonstration against the Guatemala coup. He carries her coffin under a communist flag and says afterward that it was the most tragic day of his life, that too late he understood the most wonderful part of it had been his love for her. In the same year he petitions for readmission to the Mexican Communist Party, which expelled him in 1929. The remark is his own, published years later, and the biographers repeat it with no document under it.
suggested_refs: Kahlo's lying-in-state at the Palacio de Bellas Artes under a communist flag, July 1954
sources: Widely repeated biographical tradition citing Rivera's own later published statements

stops.name: Mexico City, the marriage to Emma Hurtado
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A year after Kahlo's death he marries Emma Hurtado, who has been his dealer and agent since 1946 and holds the exclusive right to sell his work. She is his fourth wife and his fifth ceremony, counting the second marriage to Kahlo; sources that call her the third wife have lost Angelina Beloff somewhere between Paris and Mexico. In the same period he puts the blue house and everything inside it into public trust, turning a private address into the most visited painter's house in the Americas.
suggested_refs: The Galeria Diego Rivera and the Hurtado exclusive sales agreement, from 1946

stops.name: Moscow, the cancer treatment
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the trip is attested for 1955-1956 but the institution is not confirmed; Botkin Hospital is the most commonly cited candidate and is not documented in the sources reachable here. Month and day defaulted
stops.campa: Diagnosed with cancer, he goes back to Moscow for treatment and stays into 1956. The hospital is usually named as Botkin, the institution associated with Soviet care for foreign Party figures, and no source reachable in this research confirms it; the pin should be read as the most-cited candidate and not as a fact. Twenty-eight years after he stood in Red Square as a delegate of the revolution he is in the same city as a patient, with walls in Mexico waiting that he will not live to finish.
suggested_refs: The 1955-56 Soviet medical trip; institution unconfirmed
sources: General accounts of Rivera's late-life Moscow medical trip (hospital unconfirmed)

stops.name: Ostbahnhof, East Berlin: the photograph on the platform
stops.date_confidence: date attested; the pin is the Ostbahnhof, where the documented appearance occurs, and not the Academy's own address at Robert-Koch-Platz
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of March he is photographed at the Ostbahnhof in East Berlin with Rudolf Engel and Otto Nagel of the Academy of Arts of the German Democratic Republic, on the return leg from the Soviet Union by way of Czechoslovakia and Poland. He is made a corresponding member of that academy. It registers in the record as one dated appearance and nothing more. By now his health rather than a commission or a party decides where he goes, and he is on his way home.
suggested_refs: Photographs of Rivera at Berlin Ostbahnhof with Rudolf Engel and Otto Nagel, 21 March 1956

stops.name: Casa Estudio San Angel, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Spanish record gives the hour as 23:20
stops.campa: He dies at twenty past eleven at night in the O'Gorman studio, of heart failure after the cancer treatment, seventy years old. Orozco has been dead eight years and Siqueiros will outlive him by fourteen. The mural renaissance the three of them made under Vasconcelos closes here, in a concrete cube with a spiral stair, among unfinished canvases and papier mache Judases. His autobiography, dictated to Gladys March across years and running to some two thousand pages of recollection, is published in 1960.
suggested_refs: Diego Rivera with Gladys March, My Art, My Life (Citadel Press, 1960)
sources: es.wikipedia, 'Museo Casa Estudio Diego Rivera y Frida Kahlo'

stops.name: Rotonda de las Personas Ilustres, the state takes the body
stops.date_confidence: attested for the interment date; the wish about the ashes is biographical tradition and was not found in the primary record checked this session
stops.campa: Against a stated wish to have his ashes mixed with Kahlo's at Anahuacalli, the state claims the body and buries him on the twenty-sixth of November in the Rotunda of Illustrious Persons, then still called the Rotunda of Illustrious Men, among generals, presidents and poets. The wish is reported by biographers and is not in the primary record checked here. The blue house opens as the Museo Frida Kahlo the following year. The pyramid he built to hold his own ashes opens in 1964, without them in it.
suggested_refs: Rotonda de las Personas Ilustres, Panteon Civil de Dolores, Mexico City
sources: Hayden Herrera, Frida (for the ashes tradition)
